entry.evidence: However, questions remain regarding whether and how PM 2.5 concentrations directly related to atmospheric general circulation.

sequences.source_document: Published paper (XML located text and PDF)

steps.action: The authors pose the open question of whether and how surface PM2.5 relates to the atmospheric general circulation, noting that no study has linked wave activity to PM2.5.
steps.quote: However, questions remain regarding whether and how PM 2.5 concentrations directly related to atmospheric general circulation.

steps.action: They adopt the AWA-regression approach the same group developed for ozone (Sun et al. 2019) and add quantile regression for PM2.5, with detrended and deseasonalized daily residuals.
steps.quote: This study is a followup study to Sun et al. (2019), using the same approach used there to analyze ozone

steps.action: They compile summer IMPROVE PM2.5 from 150 stations (1988-2014) and ERA-Interim 500 hPa geopotential height, and choose three representative sites matched to an earlier ozone study.
steps.quote: All stations with at least 1000 valid PM 2.5 values between 1988 and 2014 are collected in this study

steps.action: They take existing CESM CAM4-Chem CCMI output: a MERRA-driven hindcast (REFC1SD), free-running current and future CO2 runs (GCM2000, GCM2100), and an RCP future-emissions run (REFC2).
steps.quote: We compare the IMPROVE data with output from the Community Earth System Model (CESM) as simulated for the Chemistry-Climate Model Initiative (CCMI)

steps.action: They compute anticyclonic local finite-amplitude wave activity from Z500 using equivalent latitude and integrals of northward contour displacement.
steps.quote: To calculate AWA, we adopt the procedures in Chen et al. (2015) and Huang and Nakamura (2016).

steps.action: They check the model premise by correlating simulated and observed monthly climatological PM2.5 at the three sites (r > 0.80).
steps.quote: for current PM 2.5 is found between observations and simulations of monthly mean climatological averages

steps.action: They map 20-year summer mean AWA and PM2.5 and their differences across scenarios (hindcast minus coupled, future minus current).
steps.quote: The 20-year averaged AWA on summer days exhibits a maximum over the southwestern US (Fig. 3a; shaded).

steps.action: They regress daily PM2.5 at three sites on AWA at every grid point and find positive coefficients near the sites.
steps.quote: the PM 2.5 concentrations are positively correlated with AWA in the areas close to the sites

steps.action: They compare the observed regression patterns with those from the hindcast and the coupled runs: the hindcast is similar, the coupled run less so.
steps.quote: Overall the model simulates similar spatial patterns to the observations for the case of the reanalysis-driven simulations (REFC1SD) but does less well

steps.action: They attribute the coupled-model mismatch to uncertain emissions, model process errors and internal variability, rather than to the AWA-PM2.5 relation.
steps.quote: which may be driving these inconsistencies between modeled and observed relationships

steps.action: They compute composite AWA for days above the 90th percentile of PM2.5, compare it with the regression maps, and justify the 90th-percentile threshold by comparing composites at other quantiles (Fig. S1).
steps.quote: The pattern for the composite AWA corresponding to daily PM 2.5 above the 90th quantile is most similar to regression coefficients

steps.action: They extend both metrics to every station and grid point across the observed and four simulated datasets, and find positive connections throughout the US.
steps.quote: PM 2.5 concentrations are positively correlated with AWA throughout the US but with varying strengths (Fig. 6).

steps.action: They propose that anticyclonic conditions (subsidence, light wind, no rain, inversions) account for the positive link.
steps.quote: which is likely accounted for by arid weather and sinking inversions

steps.action: They set the link against published stagnation-PM2.5 and ozone studies and find them consistent.
steps.quote: This is consistent with the PM 2.5 sensitivity study of Tai et al. ( [...] ).

steps.action: At AREN1 they fit linear and quantile regressions (10th-90th percentiles) of PM2.5 on impact-region AWA; the 90th-percentile slope is about 3 times the 10th, with overall r = 0.36.
steps.quote: the 90th percentile of PM 2.5 is approximately 3 times more sensitive to the averaged AWA over the impact region

steps.action: They test whether the higher-quantile sensitivity holds at all 150 sites by differencing the 90th- and 50th-percentile slopes at the 5 % level.
steps.quote: Out of the 150 sites, 145 sites show that 90th-percentile PM 2.5 increases more than the 50th percentile of PM 2.5

steps.action: They compare the quantile result with Porter et al. (2015) and find it partly consistent.
steps.quote: These results are to some extent consistent with those from Porter et al. (2015)

steps.action: In the GCM2000 run they regress interannual PM2.5 on the projection of AWA anomalies onto the regression pattern; R² reaches 0.75 depending on grid box.
steps.quote: This means that the projected value (using only AWA changes) captures up to 75 % of the interannual variability in PM 2.5

steps.action: They compare the R² values with Wise and Comrie (2005) for the southwest.
steps.quote: here we see a comparable relationships across the southwest, although these studies use different methodologies

steps.action: They predict future PM2.5 change from the projected AWA change using current-climate slopes (Eq. 7), assuming the relation is stationary.
steps.quote: Here we assume that the linear relationship between the predictors and PM 2.5 does not change very much in the future

steps.action: They compare the AWA-predicted change with the simulated GCM2100 minus GCM2000 change as a fraction; it exceeds 50 % in the western US.
steps.quote: The impact of AWA change alone on summer PM 2.5 concentrations is likely to be quite significant (above 50 %) in the western US

steps.action: They examine the future change in Z500 (Fig. S2): a 25-55 m rise with an anticyclonic pattern over the western US.
steps.quote: can account for the PM 2.5 variability resulting from changes in AWA

steps.action: They set the projected western increase against published projections of mixed sign and region, and attribute the discrepancies to differences in model formulation.
steps.quote: The discrepancy between studies mentioned above and the results given here is most likely attributable to differences in model formulation.

steps.action: They attribute the mismatch between predicted (west) and simulated (east) change to the AWA change pattern and to meteorological drivers the univariate linear model omits; they note speciation is unavailable.
steps.quote: This discrepancy mostly results from the distribution of projected AWA change (Fig. 3).

steps.action: They keep the claim that summer PM2.5 is positively linked to local AWA across the US, more strongly at high percentiles, with regional variation.
steps.quote: This analysis demonstrates that PM 2.5 is positively linked to the local anticyclonic finite-amplitude wave activity over the past 2 decades during JJA

sequences.source_document: Open discussion acp-2021-750 (RC1, AC1, RC2, AC2 and supplements)

steps.action: Referee 1 asked why the three representative sites were chosen; the authors added the matching to the Sun et al. (2017) ozone sites and the clean-air status of LAVO1.
steps.quote: How to choose the three sites (i.e., AREN1, SIPS1, and LAVO1) as the representative stations of different part of the country and why?

steps.action: Referee 1 asked for the AWA equations; the authors added equations 1-4 to Section 2.3.
steps.quote: it’s better to list the equation(s) used to calculate AWA (or LWA)

steps.action: Referee 1 asked why Wise and Comrie found lower R²; the authors tabulated the differences and added a sentence calling the results comparable despite different methods.
steps.quote: why Wise and Comrie (2005) show much lower coefficient of determinations (i.e., 0.1-0.5) than this study (i.e., 0.75)?

steps.action: Referee 1 asked for a PM2.5 comparison with Porter et al. (2015); the authors rewrote the comparison to focus on PM2.5.
steps.quote: how about the comparison of PM2.5 results in this study with that in Porter et al. (2015)?

steps.action: Referee 1 flagged swapped simulation names; the authors corrected the Figure 6 caption and clarified the Figure 9 and 10 captions.
steps.quote: Please go through the entire paper and make sure that the case terms are not messed up.

steps.action: Referee 2 asked for speciated PM2.5; the authors declined because the model output lacks speciation and deferred it to future work.
steps.quote: Without any individual treatment of speciated PM2.5

steps.action: Referee 2 asked for the mechanisms and covariance with local meteorology; the authors added the future Z500 change (Fig. S2) and literature, without quantifying covariance with local variables.
steps.quote: these correlations are never shown, quantified, nor discussed in any detail

steps.action: Referee 2 questioned the 1000-observation threshold and the year range; the authors explained the station coverage and added Table S1, without changing the selection.
steps.quote: 1000 observations between 1988 and 2014 seems like a very low threshold for data availability

steps.action: Referee 2 asked whether the free-running and specified-dynamics runs agree in overlapping years; the authors argued the years are arbitrary and that 20-year climatologies are comparable, with no new check.
steps.quote: Do the overlapping years between them (2006-2010) show good agreement in AWA?

steps.action: Referee 2 asked for a clearer composite method; the authors expanded Section 2.6 with a description and precedents.
steps.quote: This description needs some serious clarification.

steps.action: Referee 2 questioned the use of full-year monthly climatologies to validate the model instead of daily JJA comparisons; the authors kept Figure 2.
steps.quote: what is the relevance of including full annual cycles of PM2.5?

steps.action: Referee 2 questioned LAVO1 and suggested a Midwest or Great Plains site; the authors justified the existing sites and added none.
steps.quote: wouldn't it be beneficial to have at least one site within one or both of them?

steps.action: Referee 2 questioned the word 'correlation' for composites and the value of Fig. 5; the authors reworded to 'connection' and added composites at the 30th-90th quantiles (Fig. S1) to justify the 90th threshold.
steps.quote: I don't really see the benefit of including/discussing both regressions (Fig 4) and high PM2.5 filtered subset (Fig 5)

steps.action: Referee 2 asked the authors to acknowledge the weak overall correlation (r = 0.36) at AREN1; they added a sentence that other drivers dominate there.
steps.quote: it must be noted that this lack of overall correlation implies other (and likely MUCH more important) drivers

steps.action: Referee 2 asked for a formal test of the difference between the 90th- and 50th-percentile slopes; the authors applied a Z-test (Paternoster et al. 1998) and replotted Fig. 7b.
steps.quote: More robust tools to evaluate and compare quantile regression coefficients are available, and should be used to establish significance here.

steps.action: Referee 2 doubted the 75 % R² and the switch to interannual variance; the authors explained that daily R² reached only 0.56, so they reported the interannual 0.75, and added the period to the text.
steps.quote: 75% explained variability seems VERY high to my eye, given previous figures and results.

tree.answer: Yes: a positive daily link between summer PM2.5 and nearby anticyclonic wave activity
No: AWA is computed from Z500, and the link is inferred by regression and compositing
Characterize the PM2.5-AWA relation by site, region and quantile, and test its use for projection
No stated rival hypotheses; other meteorological drivers and speciation are acknowledged only
Found in the observational record; model scenarios (CO2, emissions) set by CCMI protocols

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Yes: many summer days at 150 stations and grid points, across five datasets
Mostly: holds across obs and hindcast, both metrics and 145 of 150 sites; weaker in the coupled run
Kept as a regularity for summer over the US
Published after minor and major revisions; several referee requests declined

end.claim: In US summers, daily PM2.5 is positively connected to local anticyclonic wave activity at nearly all stations; higher PM2.5 percentiles are more sensitive, and the strength varies regionally.

decisive_move.sentence: Without the regression of daily IMPROVE PM2.5 on gridded reanalysis AWA, which showed positive coefficients near the sites, there would be no relation to generalize, composite, or project.

gates.evidence: All data are archival (IMPROVE, ERA-Interim, existing CCMI runs); no hypothesis directed their acquisition. The relation could have failed in the obs-versus-model consistency checks (§3.1 ¶1), across stations (§3.3 ¶2) and in the predicted-versus-simulated future change (§3.4 ¶3, ¶6). Partial failures (coupled run, east-west mismatch) were protected by auxiliary explanations, and no null model was used beyond 5 % significance. Nothing was fixed in advance, and the review record shows the 90th-percentile threshold and interannual R² were chosen after comparing alternatives (§3.1 ¶2; AC2-S p.13).

imports.item: Influential-observation reasoning (Cook 1979) and coefficient of determination (Kutner et al. 2004)
Health effects of PM2.5 (mortality, cardiovascular) as motivation

novelty_claims.quote: However, no previous studies have investigated how wave activity can lead to changes in PM 2.5 concentrations
Such an exploration of PM 2.5 from atmospheric motion can provide new insights into understanding the mechanism of PM 2.5 changes
This study presents new perspectives to explore both the observed and simulated PM 2.5 responses to climate change.

limits: Sub-claims at other statuses: higher-quantile sensitivity (regularity_in_range, strongest in the northeast, though AREN1 has r = 0.36); up to 75 % of interannual variance explained in GCM2000 (estimate, no uncertainty given); future PM2.5 increase from AWA change in the western US, up to 0.92 µg m-3 (model-based estimate under an assumed stationary relation, no uncertainty given; closest to estimate_with_resolution but without resolution). The abstract says 'Changes between current and future climates in AWA can explain up to 75 %', but §3.4 ¶1 computes the R² from present-climate interannual variability; the mismatch is an inference from comparing the two passages. The abstract's 'up to R = 0.65' is not located in the main text. The paper does not record that the interannual R² was preferred because daily R² reached only 0.56 (AC2-S p.13); that fork appears only in the review record and is therefore not coded in alternatives_considered. The Z-test used for Fig. 7b (AC2-S p.12) is not described in the published Methods. Table 1 still lists model years for GCM2000 and GCM2100, although AC1-S p.8 says they were removed. 'Where meteorology dominates' is not defined in the paper; AC2-S p.13 defines it from LAVO1 in Fig. 2. No check of free-running against specified-dynamics AWA in overlapping years; no speciation; no quantified covariance of AWA with local meteorology; the univariate linear model omits other drivers. The conclusion that AWA is positively correlated 'at every available station' is not directly shown station by station; Fig. 7b shows 5 sites with slope differences of zero or below, by inference. Whether model simulation and composite results were planned before the observational results were seen is not stated.

disagreements.support: The AWA-predicted future PM2.5 increase sits in the western US rather than the Midwest found by Tagaris et al.
disagreements.quote: but our signal is in the west

disagreements.support: The paper projects meteorology-driven PM2.5 increases where Avise et al. found reductions; it attributes the discrepancy to model formulation without testing that.
disagreements.quote: In contrast, Avise et al. (2009) found that changes in meteorology tend to reduce summertime PM 2.5 concentrations

disagreements.target: Tagaris et al. (2007) and Racherla and Adams (2006) on the climate-only PM2.5 response
disagreements.support: Other models give small or eastern responses; the paper attributes the difference to model formulation and the lack of consistency across studies.
disagreements.quote: while Tagaris et al. (2007) found that climate change, alone, with no emissions increase or controls affects the US PM 2. [...]

disagreements.target: Simulated constant-emissions future change and Tai et al. (2012) projections
disagreements.support: The AWA-predicted change differs from the simulated change, which peaks in the east; the paper explains this by the AWA change pattern and omitted meteorological drivers.
disagreements.quote: is different from the simulated future change in PM 2.5 from the constant-emissions run, which simulate the most significant change in the eastern US

disagreements.support: Higher-quantile sensitivity agrees with Porter et al., but Porter's temperature sensitivities peak only in the east.
disagreements.quote: but with PM 2.5 sensitivities to temperature peaks entirely in the east due to the regionality of PM 2.5 speciation

disagreements.support: Their R² of 0.1-0.5 is called comparable in the southwest despite a higher maximum here, with differences in method and period noted.
disagreements.quote: although these studies use different methodologies as well as considering different time periods
